title: Jenner's smallpox vaccine: the first vaccination
summary: Edward Jenner, a country doctor in Berkeley, Gloucestershire, suspected that the pus from cowpox blisters, a mild disease caught from cows, protected people against smallpox. On 14 May 1796 he scraped material from the cowpox blisters of a milkmaid, Sarah Nelmes, into two small cuts on the arm of James Phipps, the eight-year-old son of his gardener; when Jenner later exposed the boy to smallpox matter, he did not fall ill. Jenner published his results in 1798, and his Latin name for cowpox, variolae vaccinae, gave us the words vaccine and vaccination.
why: Smallpox killed about 30 percent of the people it infected and is estimated to have killed up to 300 million people in the 20th century alone; vaccination campaigns, finished by a WHO global programme, wiped it out, and in 1980 smallpox became the only human disease ever eradicated. Jenner's idea of training the body's defences in advance grew into the vaccines that, by a 2024 WHO-led estimate, have saved at least 154 million lives in the past 50 years, 101 million of them infants.
also: An older and riskier method, variolation (infecting people with material from a mild case of smallpox itself), had been practised in China from around the 1500s and reached Europe from Asia in the early 18th century; Jenner himself was variolated as a schoolboy.

title: The electric telegraph: "What hath God wrought"
summary: With $30,000 from the US Congress, the painter-turned-inventor Samuel Morse strung two copper wires on about 700 chestnut poles beside the Baltimore and Ohio Railroad between Washington and Baltimore. On 24 May 1844, from the Supreme Court chamber in the Capitol, he tapped out the Bible phrase "What hath God wrought" in his dot-and-dash code to his partner Alfred Vail at the railway's Mount Clare station in Baltimore. It was the first long-distance overland electric telegraph in the United States.
why: For the first time a message could travel faster than a horse, a ship or a train. Within two decades telegraph wires crossed the United States (October 1861, ending the Pony Express), a cable under the Atlantic linked Europe and North America in 1866, Britain was wired to India in 1870 and Australia to the world in 1872, and a Pacific cable in 1902 encircled the globe; newspapers, markets, railways and governments began to work in near real time, and once a cable reached the Crimea in 1855, war news arrived in London within hours.
also: Morse was not alone: in Britain William Cooke and Charles Wheatstone patented a needle telegraph in 1837 that became the first commercial telegraph system, while Morse's code, in a modified form, became the international standard in 1865.

title: Electricity for cities: Edison's Pearl Street station
place: Pearl Street, Lower Manhattan, New York City (USA)
summary: On 4 September 1882 Thomas Edison's Pearl Street Station in Lower Manhattan began generating electricity from coal-fired steam engines and dynamos, sending direct current through the world's first underground urban network to light about 400 of his new incandescent lamps for some 80 customers; by 1884 it served 508 customers with 10,164 lamps. London's Holborn Viaduct station had opened the same year, and in the 1880s and 1890s engineers such as George Westinghouse switched to alternating current, which could be sent over long distances, making large power grids possible.
why: Central power stations turned electricity from a laboratory curiosity into a public utility that could light streets and homes and drive factory motors, which were several times more efficient than small steam engines. Electric power spread to most of humanity in the 20th century: 49 percent of the world's people had electricity in 1970 and 76 percent in 1990, though about 666 million people, most of them in sub-Saharan Africa, still lacked it in 2023.
also: The small town of Godalming in Surrey, England, ran what is believed to be the first public power supply in the autumn of 1881, lighting its streets with hydroelectricity, but it was not a commercial success. In the United States 95 percent of generating capacity was alternating current by 1917.

title: The Wright brothers' first powered flight
place: Kill Devil Hills, near Kitty Hawk, North Carolina (USA)
summary: On 17 December 1903, on the windy sand dunes of Kill Devil Hills near Kitty Hawk, North Carolina, Orville Wright piloted the Wright Flyer, a fabric-covered biplane with a 12-horsepower petrol engine that he and his brother Wilbur, bicycle makers from Dayton, Ohio, had built with their mechanic Charles Taylor. The first flight lasted 12 seconds and covered 37 m (120 ft); the fourth and last flight of the day, with Wilbur at the controls, covered 260 m (852 ft) in 59 seconds. It was the first sustained, controlled flight of a powered, heavier-than-air aircraft with a person aboard.
why: Within a lifetime aircraft shrank the world: Alcock and Brown flew the Atlantic in 1919, a jet aircraft flew in 1939, and humans landed on the Moon 66 years after Kitty Hawk. Air travel became a mass form of transport, with airlines carrying 4.1 billion passengers in 2017, and by the start of the First World War aircraft were already being used for reconnaissance and attacks on the ground.
also: The Wrights' key breakthrough was not the engine but control: they solved how to steer and balance an aircraft in the air with "wing warping" and a movable rudder and elevator, after testing three full-sized gliders from 1900. The original 1903 Flyer hangs in the Smithsonian's National Air and Space Museum in Washington.

title: Penicillin and the age of antibiotics
summary: In September 1928 the Scottish doctor Alexander Fleming noticed at St Mary's Hospital in London that a Penicillium mould contaminating one of his bacterial cultures had killed the bacteria around it; he called the substance penicillin, but could not purify it. In 1940 a team at the University of Oxford led by Howard Florey and Ernst Chain made concentrated penicillin and showed it cured infections, and from 1941 US laboratories and drug companies worked out how to mass-produce it, making 2.3 million doses in time for the D-Day landings in June 1944. Fleming, Florey and Chain shared the 1945 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine.
why: Penicillin was one of the first medicines that could reliably cure deadly bacterial infections such as those caused by staphylococci and streptococci; in the Second World War it greatly cut deaths and amputations from infected wounds, and after 1945 it became widely available and opened the way to many more antibiotics, making common infections, surgery and childbirth far safer. Overuse has since bred resistant bacteria, which Fleming warned of in 1945: antimicrobial resistance was directly blamed for 1.27 million deaths in 2019.
also: The best mould for mass production came from a mouldy cantaloupe melon bought in a market in Peoria, Illinois, in 1943, and yielded six times as much penicillin as Fleming's strain. Florey chose not to patent penicillin, having been advised that doing so would be unethical.

title: The first electronic computers
place: Moore School of Electrical Engineering, University of Pennsylvania, Philadelphia (USA)
summary: ENIAC (Electronic Numerical Integrator and Computer), built in secret for the US Army by John Mauchly and J. Presper Eckert at the University of Pennsylvania, was completed in 1945 and put to work on 10 December that year; it was the first programmable, electronic, general-purpose digital computer. It filled a room, weighed about 27 tonnes and used about 18,000 vacuum tubes, could calculate about a thousand times faster than electromechanical machines, and was programmed with switches and cables by six women mathematicians, among them Kay McNulty, Betty Jennings and Betty Snyder. In Britain, the codebreakers at Bletchley Park had already used Colossus, a programmable electronic machine designed by Tommy Flowers, from early 1944 to read German high-command messages, though it was built for that single job and kept secret until the 1970s.
why: Electronic computers turned calculation, and later almost all information, into something machines could process at enormous speed. The transistor, invented at Bell Labs in 1947, replaced fragile, power-hungry vacuum tubes and let computers shrink from rooms to chips; more than 13 sextillion MOS transistors had been manufactured by 2018, making them the most numerous artificial objects in history, and they run everything from phones and cars to banks, hospitals and power grids.
also: ENIAC's first program was a study for the hydrogen bomb, not the artillery tables it was built for. Germany's Konrad Zuse had completed the electromechanical Z3 computer in Berlin in 1941.

title: The structure of DNA: the double helix
summary: On 25 April 1953 the journal Nature published a short paper by James Watson and Francis Crick of the Cavendish Laboratory in Cambridge proposing that DNA, the molecule that carries genetic information, is a double helix: two strands twisted around each other, held together by pairs of bases in which A always pairs with T and C with G. Their model drew heavily on X-ray diffraction images made at King's College London by Rosalind Franklin and her student Raymond Gosling, above all "Photo 51" of May 1952, which Maurice Wilkins showed Watson without their knowledge; papers by the King's groups appeared in the same issue.
why: The structure explained at once how living things copy and pass on their genetic instructions, since each strand can serve as a template for a new partner, a point the paper noted in its famous last line. It transformed biology, enabled researchers to understand the genetic code, and led to the Human Genome Project, which read most of the human DNA sequence by 2003 at a cost of about $2.7 billion.
also: Watson, Crick and Wilkins received the 1962 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine; Franklin had died in 1958, and the Nobel Committee never makes posthumous nominations.

title: The Internet: ARPANET and TCP/IP
summary: At 10:30 pm on 29 October 1969, UCLA student programmer Charley Kline tried to log in from a computer in Boelter Hall to a computer at the Stanford Research Institute over ARPANET, a network funded by the US Defense Department that broke messages into small "packets"; the remote machine crashed after two characters, so the first message ever sent was "lo", and the login worked about an hour later. During the 1970s Vint Cerf and Bob Kahn designed TCP/IP, a common set of rules that let separate networks join into one "network of networks", and on 1 January 1983, "flag day", ARPANET switched over to it for good, giving the Internet its common language.
why: TCP/IP lets any computer network connect to any other, with no central control, so the Internet could grow from four computers in 1969 and 213 in 1981 to a single worldwide system. With the World Wide Web, email and later smartphones running on top of it, an estimated 6 billion people, about three-quarters of humanity, were using the Internet in 2025, transforming how people communicate, learn, shop, work and organise, although 2.2 billion remain offline.
also: The World Wide Web, invented at CERN in 1989, is a service that runs on the Internet, not the Internet itself. ARPANET drew on the packet-switching ideas of Paul Baran in the US and Donald Davies in Britain.

title: The smartphone: the iPhone puts the Internet in every pocket
summary: On 9 January 2007, at the Macworld conference in San Francisco, Apple's Steve Jobs unveiled the iPhone as "a widescreen iPod with touch controls", "a revolutionary mobile phone" and "a breakthrough Internet communicator" in one device; it went on sale in the United States on 29 June 2007. It dropped the physical keyboard and stylus for a multi-touch screen worked with the fingers, and in July 2008 Apple opened the App Store, letting outside developers sell programs for it. Google's Android phones soon followed the same pattern.
why: The smartphone turned the phone into a pocket computer, camera, map, wallet and window on the Internet. Smartphones outsold ordinary mobile phones by early 2013, when shipments passed 1 billion a year, and by 2025 82 percent of people aged 10 and over owned a mobile phone. In countries such as India, Kenya, South Africa, the Philippines and Pakistan most Internet users went online by phone rather than by computer, and in 2008 mobile phones overtook personal computers as the most common way to reach the Internet.
also: Earlier smartphones, such as BlackBerry's, were aimed mainly at business users and relied on keyboards or styluses; the iPhone was aimed at the general public and quickly became Apple's most successful product.

title: Generative AI: ChatGPT
summary: On 30 November 2022 the San Francisco company OpenAI released ChatGPT, a chatbot, free to use in its basic form, built on a large language model, a generative pre-trained transformer (GPT) trained on huge amounts of text, that could answer questions, write essays and computer code, translate and summarise in everyday language. The models behind it rest on the transformer, a design introduced in 2017 by eight Google researchers in the paper "Attention Is All You Need", which has since been cited more than 150,000 times. ChatGPT gained one million users in five days and 100 million in two months, then the fastest growth of any internet application.
why: ChatGPT brought artificial intelligence that can produce text, images and code into everyday use and sped up an AI boom of rapid investment and public attention; by February 2026 it had 900 million weekly users. It has raised hopes of transforming many professions, and debate over the future of work, cheating in education, misinformation, copyright and the confident but false answers known as "hallucinations".
also: Transformers were first built to improve machine translation; their "attention" mechanism lets a model weigh how every word in a passage relates to every other, which turned out to work for many other tasks.
